pr_title: Container Interface: expose the host's os-release metadata to nspawn and portable guests
pr_body:
As discussed on the mailing thread and RFE, here's a stab at implementing this feature via container_host_KEY=VALUE environment variables.

Thoughts?

Fixes #15878
pr_comments: Added a paragraph in man/os-release.xml too - assuming it is ok, it seemed worth mentioning there as well.

Why do you want to leak host os info by default into a container? Especially for the case where you're booting another full distro and not just running an application in the container that seems extremely weird.

> Why do you want to leak host os info by default into a container? Especially for the case where you're booting another full distro and not just running an application in the container that seems extremely weird.

Hello Christian, thanks for having a look at this.

The idea is that this already happens - both because most of the information is already available via uname, and because I counted 4 different ways this is done today in various environments. Since os-release is a standard interface, that does not contain privileged information, the thought was that it would be quite nice to have a common interface that an application can rely upon. https://systemd.io/CONTAINER_INTERFACE/ seemed the natural place to start.

Of course most ~container-like runtime managers, if not all, already allow to set arbitrary environment variables or arbitrary bind mounts, so it's not so much about a missing capability, but more about having a common, predefined way of accessing information that is not provided by a user or an administrator or an orchestrator - it is fixed, and well defined.

I'm also not arguing that this isn't done or can be useful sometimes. My questions is first and foremost why do it by default.
If a user spawns a container the default assumption is that information leaks from the host into the container is minimized. That's the part the runtime should guarantee. We even have a tiny fuse filesystem that virtualizes uptime, cpuinfo and various other files for you.
The other expectation is that tools inside of a container should make as little assumptions about the host from inside the container as possible. Specifically, they shouldn't alter their behavior inside of a container depending on the host. That sounds like an invitation to disaster in the long run.

I'm afraid these particular horses have bolted the stable long, long ago :-) Especially in datacentres, it is quite common for anything that has to do any host management of any kind to alter behavior depending on where it's running. I see it all the time in Azure. It's not something new, and it's not something that will go away anytime soon either. As @stgraber has said, I'd be very careful in what is exposed. This seems a slippery slope potentially leading information to be exposed that can be used for container escapes/exploits.

the personality thing doesn't hide the kernel version from uname, which is the really interesting part of the information from uname, i.e. what allows you to identify the host OS easily.

I don't think runtime parameters/configuration from the host OS should be leaked into the container either (but of course, in reality they massively are leaked into it, because of sysfs, which carries so much info about the kernel, its current state and its current configuration). What @bluca proposed here isn't runtime parameters though, it really is static OS vendor and version info only (because that's what /etc/os-release contains). And this distinction between "static OS vendor data" and "runtime data/configuration" is what is key here. The distinction is precisely what personality/CLONE_NEWUTS allow you to hide from the container and what they do not allow you to hide from the container. i.e. uname -r is static vendor data, and thus is unaffected by personality/CLONE_NEWUTS. But uname -n/-m/… are dynamic runtime parameters and thus can be detached from the host through personality/CLONE_NEWUTS...

The reason I think it's fine if we pass this data along by default in nspawn is that the info from the host's /etc/os-release can be determined from inside the container anyway, and it's not secret data anyway. I'd rather have a well-defined interface that *just* *works* where people look this data up, which is a nicely defined, well-known entrypoint to this kind of stuff (and thus can be easily controlled, turned-off, replaced, updated) than have people grepping all over /sys and determining the info about the host OS via ugly hacks in an uncontrolled way.

These are just my thoughts for nspawn however, and nspawn has a much more "batteries included" approach than LXC, i.e. we will set up things a certain way for you and make much less configurable, and a lot more opt-out than opt-in than LXC, which is more a set of low-level tools you can put together in a gazillion different ways. Hence, what I think makes sense to just do for nspawn here, might be something for LXC you want to make opt-in or not at all (and thus leave it to the user to do this manually).

I mean, let me underline this: if @bluca's patch would start importing host runtime settings — which it does not —, such as hostname, or network config or so into the containers I'd not merge it either. I am just fine with the OS vendor data to be pulled in, as that's not secret data really, and static, and can be retrieved otherwise anyway.

> the personality thing doesn't hide the kernel version from uname, which is the really interesting part of the information from uname, i.e. what allows you to identify the host OS easily.

The arch is very much relevant especially with all the arm versions that exist.

```

> cat /etc/os-release 
NAME="Ubuntu"
VERSION="20.04 LTS (Focal Fossa)"

ID_LIKE=debian

controlled, turned-off, replaced, updated) than have people grepping all over /sys and determining the info about the host OS via ugly hacks in an uncontrolled way.

sysfs leaks device info but it's all nobody:nogroup and any real info leak is a kernel bug and is always fixed. In addition, the container can simply be prevented from mounting sysfs at which point it isn't accessible anymore which some users tend to do.

I am just fine with the OS vendor data to be pulled in, as that's not secret data really, and static, and can be retrieved otherwise anyway.

This is a rather fundamental question. If you're talking about sandboxing ala portable services then this leakage is probably fine as it's not intended to be really isolated or at least only be partially isolated. But e.g. full system containers with all namespaces have no business leaking any host info into the container by default; static or dynamic, or whether or not a namespace covers it isn't really relevant. This becomes even more problematic when thinking about nested containers.

(Let alone the fact that the tools are broken that need these assumptions and standardizing around them isn't a great idea in the first place. That static info encourages tools to make _standardized_ assumptions about their behavior outside of the container and that's not great. The point is tools should care as little as possible about running in a container or not; systemd included and it's doing a great job at it mostly.)

> sysfs leaks device info but it's all nobody:nogroup and any real info leak is a kernel bug and is always fixed. In addition, the container can simply be prevented from mounting sysfs at which point it isn't accessible anymore which some users tend to do.

Oh, it leaks info in very simple, obvious ways. For example: does "test -f /sys/fs/selinux/" exist? yes, then there's a very high probability that the host runs fedora/rhel/centos family of distros. do you find cgroupvs1 or cgroupsv2 mounted? depending on what you know which version of the distro. /sys/hypervisor tells you everything about the stuff even surrounding the kernel... /sys/module/ tells you which modules are available and built in, which tells you pretty exactly what distro you are looking at because it's a fingerprint of the kernel config. 

Now, the stuff @bluca wants to pass along is all the stuff you can derive with heuristics from /sys/, but in an explicit form, i.e. doesn't require you to do fingerprinting. So I'd argue, the information you get that way is not worse than what uname() and /sys tell you anyway about the OS surrounding it.

>  brauner@wittgenstein|~
> > cat /etc/os-release 
> NAME="Ubuntu"
> VERSION="20.04 LTS (Focal Fossa)"
> ID=ubuntu
> ID_LIKE=debian
> PRETTY_NAME="Ubuntu 20.04 LTS"
> VERSION_ID="20.04"
> HOME_URL="https://www.ubuntu.com/"
> SUPPORT_URL="https://help.ubuntu.com/"
> BUG_REPORT_URL="https://bugs.launchpad.net/ubuntu/"
> PRIVACY_POLICY_URL="https://www.ubuntu.com/legal/terms-and-policies/privacy-policy"
> VERSION_CODENAME=focal
> UBUNTU_CODENAME=focal

the patch from @bluca only deals with the "_ID" fields of that, i.e. only with ID= and VERSION_ID= fields from ubuntu's /etc/os-release. if you have "uname -r", then it's very easy to look up the right /etc/os-release that comes with the distro that comes with that kernel...

> sysfs leaks device info but it's all nobody:nogroup and any real info leak is a kernel bug and is always fixed. In addition, the container can simply be prevented from mounting sysfs at which point it isn't accessible anymore which some users tend to do.

Given how much of the Linux API is exposed through /sys/ hiding it entirely means you basically take away a major chunk of the Linux API. Which might be fine for specific apps, but I doubt it's a good idea if you want to keep compat with general purpose OS images, i.e. images that run systemd inside of them. I mean, that's the point I am making with the "batteries included" comment: in nspawn you get /sys in the container, read-only with a few things taken away, but there's definitely more there than is missing. and it's not a configurable option. You cannot opt-out of it. And in such an environment I think it's fine if people get the _ID fields from /etc/os-release passed in too, to make things easy, so that you don't have to maintain your own database that maps "uname -r" back to the distro version that shipped that specific kernel...

But again, I am not arguing whether LXC should do the same thing. LXC exposes a lot more low-level options, it doesn't make choices for users like nspawn does. That's totally fine, hence what is OK in nspawn, i.e. that we just pass it right-away doesn't have to be fine for LXC, that's something you have to figure out.

> This is a rather fundamental question. If you're talking about sandboxing ala portable services then this leakage is probably fine as it's not intended to be really isolated or at least only be partially isolated. But e.g. full system containers with all namespaces have no business leaking any host info into the container by default; static or dynamic, or whether or not a namespace covers it isn't really relevant. This becomes even more problematic when thinking about nested containers.

So, in your own example above, you leaked into the container uname -r as `5.7.0-rc6-brauner-seccomp-notify-empt`. Which tells me a lot about your host system. Really a lot. As far as I know there's no functionality available in the Linux kernel currently to hide uname -r from a container. Are you working on adding something like that, then? do you consider that information leakage you'd like to address?

btw, lxc also sets $container=lxc iirc. Which we use to make our "ConditionVirtualization=lxc" unit file setting work. by your standards, that'd be information leakage to you'd like to remove? if you leak the fact that lxc is used into the container, is it so much worse to also leak the host os ID and VERSION_ID into it?

> I'd rather have a well-defined interface that just works where people look this data up, which is a nicely defined, well-known entrypoint to this kind of stuff (and thus can be easily controlled, turned-off, replaced, updated) than have people grepping all over /sys and determining the info about the host OS via ugly hacks in an uncontrolled way.

I think this is a good emphasis to put on this feature request:

* primarily, have an interface/convention: *if* you want to share this information with the container, then here is how you do it;
* secondarily, give systemd's own container interfaces (-nspawn and portable services) an option to enable sharing this information (the default could either be on or off), or even make them share this information unconditionally if desired - which of these is chosen depends on the systemd maintainers' policies

Other container frameworks like lxc and Flatpak can choose whether to share this information (never, or off-by-default, or on-by-default, or unconditionally) according to *their* policies, and might come up with a different answer - but in the cases where they *do* decide to share it, if the interface/convention is the same, everyone wins.

Similarly, if a container framework like Docker doesn't participate in this interface/convention, but is sufficiently configurable that its users can make individual container instances implement the convention anyway, then it's helpful for the convention to exist so that each user doesn't have to invent their own. We have this today with `docker run --env=container=docker ...`, and we could have it in this RFC with `docker run --env=container_host_NAME="Debian GNU/Linux" ...` or `docker run --mount=type=bind,source=/etc/os-release,destination=/run/host/etc/os-release ...`, depending which convention is chosen.

As some context for my interest in this, I'm currently working on pressure-vessel, a Flatpak-derived mechanism to put Steam games in containers. This is not a security boundary at all, only an attempt to improve stability/robustness by sharing as little of the host /usr as possible - but for some things like the graphics driver, we currently have no choice other than sharing things about the host, which means we want to know what we're sharing with when people report bugs. So we've taught our diagnostic tool to look at `/run/host/etc/os-release` and `/run/host/usr/lib/os-release`, which happens to work acceptably for pressure-vessel and for some configurations of Flatpak.

> here's a stab at implementing this feature via container_host_KEY=VALUE environment variables

(I am not a systemd maintainer, systemd maintainers might overrule me on this.)

If the environment variable route is preferred, one thing that ought to be resolved is what is meant to happen about inheritance. Presumably container-runners that participate in this interface are expected to set these variable's on the container's top process (pid 1, if the container has its own pid namespace). Is the container's top process, which might be some sort of init, meant to let the environment variables propagate down to the descendant processes that run user code? Or are descendants meant to look in `/proc/1/environ` (as they would for the current `container` and `container_ttys` variables), which might require more privileges than an arbitrary descendant process normally has? Or what?

I personally still prefer the bind-mount-in-/run/host approach that I suggested on the mailing list. This avoids the inheritance question, and avoids having to care about the quoting (whatever quoting was valid in the host is equally valid in the container). It also works in Flatpak already (if you happen to have configured it to expose the host's /usr and/or /etc), works in pressure-vessel (currently unconditionally, because pressure-vessel isn't a security boundary), and can be made to work in Docker with O(1) command-line options to `docker run` (as opposed to O(n) command-line options for the environment variables).

> Or are descendants meant to look in /proc/1/environ (as they would for the current container and container_ttys variables), which might require more privileges than an arbitrary descendant process normally has?

One possibility would be to define more than one interface for reading these fields, analogous to the way systemd copies pid 1's `$container` into `/run/systemd/container` - so that diagnostic tools inside the container could try reading `/run/container-host-os-release` (or something) if they can't read pid 1's environment, and the init system inside the container could populate that file from its own environment if it isn't already a bind-mount. Or something.

> > Or are descendants meant to look in /proc/1/environ (as they would for the current container and container_ttys variables), which might require more privileges than an arbitrary descendant process normally has?
> 
> One possibility would be to define more than one interface for reading these fields, analogous to the way systemd copies pid 1's `$container` into `/run/systemd/container` - so that diagnostic tools inside the container could try reading `/run/container-host-os-release` (or something) if they can't read pid 1's environment, and the init system inside the container could populate that file from its own environment if it isn't already a bind-mount. Or something.

Very good point about descendant processes, and your suggestion sounds good to me. @poettering and other systemd devs, what do you think?

Regarding bind mounting vs env vars, as mentioned in the email thread my preference is for the latter as it allows to trivially and effortlessly look at the inner os-release at the same time, without key clashes. Having a separate file with the same keys require some logic around it. Also, it matches what the interface already specifies for the container runtime name and uuid - they are set as env vars.

But it is only a soft preference, and I'm happy to implement it the other way if there's more consensus around that.

As i said in https://github.com/systemd/systemd/issues/15878#issuecomment-640416532, I personally prefer passing host details via the filesystem, not env vars, and will do that in flatpak. (Actually do already).

> As i said in [#15878 (comment)](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/issues/15878#issuecomment-640416532), I personally prefer passing host details via the filesystem, not env vars, and will do that in flatpak. (Actually do already).

Thanks for chipping in.

Given there is a very strong preference expressed here, @poettering is it ok for your to change the implementation? If so, I'll do all the required work.
Thanks!

Hmm, so the `$container` thing is an env var, which we inherited from LXC actually. Does flatpak/bubblewrap set that at all? i mean, it's more an app sandbox than a true container env vars, but I guess the lines are blurry there...

@alexlarsson what precisely do you intend to make available in /run/host besides os-release?

systemd as PID 1 is very strict on env vars: we basically eat up all env vars, and do not allow them to be inherited down the tree further. But of course a bubblewrap-style sandbox is unlikely to run systemd as its payload PID 1 (probably can't even), hence I can see that env vars are less than ideal there...

If flatpak/bubblewrap want to go the /run/host/ route I'd be up to supporting that. 

That said, I wouldn't mind additionally going the env var route for nspawn. After all we have a slightly different focus for nspawn (i.e. we focus more on payload PID 1 being a full init system, such as systemd), and we already do the `$container=` env var thing, and thus I doubt that `$container_os_id` wouldn't be too terrible to support too. It's just a minor step.

It's up to you @bluca I guess, what you personally care about.

Flatpak never sets $container. 

As for /run/host, what exactly gets put there by flatpak depends on the permissions of the app.

If you don't have any permissions, you get the following (exact path depends on system config):

System and per-user fonts:
```
/run/host/font-dirs.xml - remap info for fonts dirs
/run/host/fonts => /usr/share/fonts
/run/host//fonts-cache => usr/lib/fontconfig/cache/
/run/host/user-fonts => ~/.fonts
/run/host//user-fonts-cache => ~/.cache/fontconfig
```
Icons:
```
/run/host/share/icons/ => /usr/share/icons
/run/host/user-share/icons/ => ~/.local/share/icons
```

Then we have a custom directory `/run/host/monitor/` which points to copies of resolve and timezone setup files that are copies of the host config, used to update these dynamically (unlike a bind mount) like so:
```
lrwxrwxrwx 1 alex alex 29 Jun 11 11:37 /etc/resolv.conf -> /run/host/monitor/resolv.conf
```

These are all kinda special to desktop use where we want to always expose certain things from the host which we believe are safe and useful.

Additionally, if your filesystem access has "host" (full access), or "host-os", then we mount the host `/usr` on `/run/host/usr`, as well as `/run/host/lib`, `/run/host/lib32`, etc.  And if permissions has "host" or "host-etc", then we also mount the host `/etc` as `/run/host/etc`.

The latest is what's being discussed in here. I guess we could in the non-permissive case mount a subset of `/run/host/etc`, such as only `/etc/os-release`, but we don't currently do that, instead an app that needs that would have to request `host-etc` access.

Thank you all. I'll switch to /run/host for everything, and as requested by Lennart also container_version_id exclusively for nspawn.
I'll work on portabled/nspawn first, then flatpak.

Pushed new revision with the above changes, tested them locally. Removed the RFC from the PR title as I believe we have reached enough consensus.
Rebased to fix merge conflict.

I am unclear about how the discussion ended.
Is this now Opt-out or Opt-in?
FWIW, I agree that however small a thing this is, it should be opt-in to release such information.
The specification allows the implementations to do this or not, i.e. it is opt-in. systemd-nspawn does this unconditionally though.

As mentioned in the discussion, such static vendor info is already released and always has been, just in convoluted ways:

```
$ sudo build/systemd-nspawn --register=no --directory /tmp/img cat /proc/sys/kernel/version
Spawning container img on /tmp/img.
Press ^] three times within 1s to kill container.
#1 SMP Debian 4.19.131-2 (2020-07-11)
Container img exited successfully.
```
```
$ sudo build/systemd-nspawn --register=no --directory /tmp/img uname -a
Spawning container img on /tmp/img.
Press ^] three times within 1s to kill container.
Linux img 4.19.0-10-amd64 #1 SMP Debian 4.19.131-2 (2020-07-11) x86_64 GNU/Linux
Container img exited successfully.
```

This is enough on all distros to pin-point exactly which distro version the host is running, using public available repository metadata.

In case one wished to build their own kernel to strip out that static vendor info for any reason, then adding the following parameters to systemd-nspawn seems pretty trivial in comparison:

```
$ sudo build/systemd-nspawn --register=no --directory /tmp/img --bind /dev/null:/run/host/etc/os-release --bind /dev/null:/run/host/usr/lib/os-release cat /run/host/etc/os-release
Spawning container img on /tmp/img.
Press ^] three times within 1s to kill container.

Container img exited successfully.
```

How about this - I'll send a follow-up that also makes the $container_host_* env variables overridable from the command line, just like the bind mounts and the $container variable are.

So, there seem to be a misunderstanding about what this patch does.

Systemd (as in PID1) is not involved in container security. PID1 is already inside the container so any info available to PID1 
is available to any application in the container with enough privilege. Anything that wants to hide stuff to  a container needs to work "below" systemd. i.e: the container manager.

What this patch does is that IF the container manager wants to provide information about the host to the container, THEN there 
is a standardized way to do so, which will allow any application to find that info in a way that is independant from the container manager.

So the "opt-in/out" option has to be at the container-manager level, not at the systemd level. 

(as a side note, the CM needs to explicitely provide the info, so any CM that is not aware of the change will not provide the info)
systemd-nspawn is a container manager, even if systemd-the-pid-1 isn't. The code changes in this MR are mostly to systemd-nspawn.

issue_context.title: RFE: common interface to expose host's os-release to container-like runtimes
issue_context.body:
Creating an RFE as requested based on the following mail thread:

https://lists.freedesktop.org/archives/systemd-devel/2020-April/044378.html

>We find ourselves in a situation where application running
containerized (specifically as portable services, although this issue
is general) need to either find information about the host, or alter
their behaviour depending on the host's flavour.
At the same time, applications also need to find information about the
guest's OS, so simply bind mounting /etc/os-release from the host is
not enough. We need both.

Proposed solutions:

- mount/copy the host's os-release in a specific path
  - Flatpak exposes files from the host under /run/host, so following that model it would look like /run/host/usr/lib/os-release
  - nspawn exposes mounts from the host in /run/systemd/nspawn/incoming, so following that model it would look like /run/systemd/nspawn/incoming/usr/lib/os-release
- have the runtime manager parse the *_ID keys from the host's os-release and make them available as environment variables to the guest, and have this as part of the container interface
comments: In https://github.com/systemd/systemd/pull/15891 the design veered toward having the runtime set an environment variable for each key in the host's os-release, prefixed by service_host_ for lightweight-container-like runtimes (portabled, flatpak, nspawn with start_pid1/2) and container_host_ for vm-like runtimes (nspawn with a full image boot, lxd)

For flatpak, I want to go with the /run/host model, because a filesystem option like that is much more robust. For example, env-vars are often cleared or changed when children are spawned, which would lose this information. Also, having the sandbox tool parse a file unnecessarily means its more risky, and less flexible (i.e. harder to extend).

review_comments: `/etc/os-release` is often a symlink to `/usr/lib/os-release`. We could optimize this by skipping /etc/os-release in that case.

Very often in the real world I've seen applications just go for /etc/os-release and bomb out if it's not there, which is of course incorrect. I've done my best to get it sorted when I've spotted it.
Perhaps if the host doesn't have it, we could symlink it in the guest's view? ../../etc/os-release -> /run/host/usr/lib/os-release
we use // for "FIXME" style comments, and /* */ for explanatory comments. See CODING_STYLE
